questions.q:
Statement 1: A burning candle is a luminous object even when it stands in a brightly lit room.
Statement 2: LED lamps are brighter and last longer than traditional lamps but consume more power.
Statement 3: Fire made by burning oil, wax or gas is a kind of artificial lighting.
Which statements are correct?
questions.a: 1 and 3 only. A candle emits its own light whatever the room is like, and fire from fuels is artificial lighting; LED lamps consume much less power, so Statement 2 is false.
o: 1 and 3 only
1 and 2 only
2 and 3 only
1, 2 and 3

questions.q: A student wrote these cards in the wrong order: electric bulb, fire made from animal fat and oil, natural fire seen after a lightning strike, LED lamp, fire first created by humans. Give the order in which these sources came into human use and say what each new step improved or made possible.
questions.a: Order: natural fire (from lightning, only observed), fire created by humans (earliest artificial light), fire from different fuels like animal fat, oil, wax and gas, electric light after electricity was invented, and LED lamps as modern electric sources. Electricity met most lighting needs; LED lamps use much less power, are brighter and last longer.
s: Correct order of the five
Fuels widened the fire sources; electricity now meets most lighting needs
LED lamps consume less power, are brighter, last longer

questions.q:
Assertion (A): If sunlight were completely blocked from reaching the Moon, we would not see the Moon shining.
Reason (R): The Moon does not emit its own light.
questions.a: Both A and R are true and R explains A. The Moon only reflects sunlight, so with no sunlight falling on it there is nothing to reflect.
o: Both A and R are true and R explains A
Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true

questions.q: In a dark hall a guard switches on his torch and points it at a polished brass bell hanging on the wall; the bell shines brightly. He then switches the torch off and nothing else in the hall is lit. What does he see of the bell, and why?
questions.a: The bell no longer shines, as it only sent back the torch light. A non-luminous object is seen only by the light that falls on it and is reflected.
o: The bell no longer shines, as it only sent back the torch light
The bell goes on shining a little, because every shiny object keeps emitting its own light after the torch is off
The bell shines even more, because a non-luminous object glows brighter once light has fallen on it for a while
The bell turns into a shadow, because the torch light that falls on it is now blocked and cannot be seen

questions.q:
(a) A firefly is a natural luminous source and a toy LED firefly clipped on a jar is an artificial one. Do both emit their own light?
(b) Which of the two belongs to the chapter's 'certain animals' that emit their own light?
questions.a: (a) Yes: both emit their own light, so both are luminous. (b) The real firefly, which is one of the certain animals that emit their own light, a natural source.
s: Part (a): both emit their own light
Part (b): the real firefly as a natural source

questions.q: Arun says, 'LED lamps are good for the environment, so when they stop working they can be thrown in the garbage like any other old bulb.' Do you agree? Explain.
questions.a: Partly. He is right that LED lamps are good for the environment, since they consume much less power. He is wrong about the garbage: at the end of their life LED lamps must be appropriately disposed of or recycled and not thrown in the garbage.
s: Verdict: partly agrees
LED lamps are better for the environment because they use much less power
Must be disposed of or recycled, not thrown in the garbage

questions.q: A resort near a forest noted this in one year: floodlights on all night around the cottages; 40 trees felled for new cottages; visitors per week tripled. Fireflies there are fewer. Which pairing of these three records with the causes the chapter gives for fewer fireflies is correct?
questions.a: Floodlights: light pollution; trees felled: reduced forest cover; tripled visitors: excessive tourism. These are the three causes named in the chapter's opening story.
o: Floodlights: light pollution; trees felled: reduced forest cover; tripled visitors: excessive tourism
Floodlights: excessive tourism; trees felled: light pollution; tripled visitors: reduced forest cover
Floodlights: reduced forest cover; trees felled: excessive tourism; tripled visitors: light pollution
Floodlights: light pollution; trees felled: excessive tourism; tripled visitors: reduced forest cover

questions.q: A hall has 40 traditional lamps of 60 W each. They are all replaced by 40 LED lamps of 10 W each giving the same brightness. The total power drawn by the hall falls by ___ W.

A panchayat will hold a three-day mela at the edge of a forest where fireflies are seen every summer. It can light the ground with (i) many traditional lamps, (ii) LED lamps, or (iii) a few LED lamps shielded to point only at the stalls. Rank these three for the mela, saying how each fares on electricity use and on the fireflies, and add what must be done with the lamps afterwards.
questions.a: Best is (iii): LED lamps use much less power and the shielding keeps light away from the forest, so there is less light pollution. Next is (ii): LED lamps save power but unshielded light still causes light pollution. Last is (i): traditional lamps use more power and give no protection from light pollution. After the mela, failed LED lamps must be disposed of or recycled properly, not thrown in the garbage; crowds should also be limited to avoid excessive tourism.
s: Ranks the shielded LED option first with the reason of less power
Shielding reduces light pollution for fireflies
Places the unshielded LED option second with a reason
Places the traditional lamps last with a reason
Proper disposal or recycling of LED lamps

questions.q:
(a) A forest fire is started by lightning, and a village gas lamp is lit with a match. Say whether each is a natural or an artificial luminous source, with a reason.
(b) Why is the first one still luminous even though it is dangerous and not useful for lighting a house?
questions.a: (a) The forest fire is a natural source because it occurs on its own in nature; the gas lamp is artificial because humans made the fire with a fuel. (b) Luminous means emitting its own light; whether it is useful or safe does not matter.
s: Part (a): natural for the forest fire, artificial for the gas lamp, with reasons
Part (b): luminous depends only on emitting its own light

questions.q:
(a) Name the cause of the fall in firefly numbers that floodlights near a forest add to.
(b) A village switches off all floodlights near the forest but keeps felling trees and allowing large crowds. Will firefly numbers recover? Give a reason.
questions.a: (a) Light pollution. (b) Not fully: reduced forest cover and excessive tourism are also causes, so removing one cause does not remove the others.
s: Part (a): light pollution
Part (b): other causes remain, so not a full recovery

questions.q: Four children list sources of light from a forest evening. Asha: a firefly and lightning. Binoy: a firefly and a wax candle. Chetan: lightning and a street LED lamp. Divya: the Sun and the Moon. Whose list contains only natural sources of light?
questions.a: Asha's list. A firefly and lightning both emit their own light and occur in nature; the candle and LED lamp are artificial, and the Moon is not a source that emits light.
o: Asha's list
Binoy's list
Chetan's list
Divya's list

questions.q: True or False: If the Sun suddenly stopped emitting light at exactly 12:00 noon, a person standing outside would still see sunshine at 12:05.
questions.a: True. Light from the Sun takes about 8 minutes 20 seconds (500 seconds) to reach the Earth, so at 12:05 (300 seconds later) the last light emitted is still arriving.
s: Verdict: True
Reason: light takes about 8 min 20 s to reach Earth, and 5 min is less than that

questions.q:
(a) At night, Venus and the Pole Star look equally bright dots. If the Sun's light stopped falling on both, what would happen to each?
(b) Which one is luminous, and what does this show about judging an object by its brightness?
questions.a: (a) Venus would no longer be seen because it only reflects sunlight; the Pole Star would carry on shining because it emits its own light. (b) The Pole Star is luminous; brightness alone does not tell us whether an object emits light or reflects it.
s: Part (a): Venus disappears, the star continues
Part (b): star luminous; brightness does not decide

questions.q: Priya says, 'The Sun is a natural source of light and a kerosene lamp is an artificial one, but both are luminous.' Her friend adds, 'The Moon is a natural source of light too, because it is found in nature and lights up the night.' Which judgement fits the chapter?
questions.a: Priya is right; the friend is wrong, since the Moon only reflects the Sun's light. Luminous objects emit their own light, and they may be natural or artificial.
o: Priya is right; the friend is wrong, since the Moon only reflects the Sun's light
Priya is wrong, because only natural objects can be luminous and a lamp made by humans cannot emit light of its own
Both are right, because anything found in nature that is bright and lights up the night is a natural source of light
Both are wrong, because the Sun reflects light from the stars and so is not luminous at all itself

questions.q: A museum shows an oil lamp, a wax candle, a gas lantern and an LED bulb. A visitor says, 'All four emit their own light, and only the LED bulb is artificial because the other three are old.' What is the correct reply?
questions.a: All four are luminous, and all four are artificial sources. Fire made with fuels such as oil, wax and gas, and electric lamps, are artificial lighting.
o: All four are luminous, and all four are artificial sources
All four are luminous, but only the oil lamp and the candle are natural sources because they are old
Only the LED bulb is luminous, because the others burn fuel and do not emit light of their own
None is luminous, because artificial objects only reflect the light that falls on them

questions.q:
Suresh runs a homestay in a Western Ghats village. In the 60-night summer season guests come to watch fireflies flash along a forest path, using small LED torches. Plan X: bright floodlights along the path and 200 guests a night at Rs 500 each. Plan Y: no floodlights, torches only, and 30 guests a night at Rs 800 each. Suppose that under Plan X the fireflies vanish after 25 nights and guests then stop coming, while under Plan Y the fireflies stay all season.
(a) A guest shines his LED torch on a rock and says the rock is luminous because it is bright. Correct him.
(b) Name the two causes of falling firefly numbers that Plan X adds.
(c) Find the season's earnings under each plan.
(d) Which plan would you advise? Weigh the money against what the guests come for.
questions.a: (a) The rock only reflects the torch light; it does not emit light, so it is non-luminous. (b) Plan X adds light pollution (floodlights) and excessive tourism (200 guests a night). (c) Plan X: 25 x (200 x 500) = Rs 25,00,000; Plan Y: 60 x (30 x 800) = Rs 14,40,000. (d) Plan X earns Rs 10,60,000 more, but it destroys the fireflies that bring the guests and leaves nothing for the next seasons; Plan Y earns less but protects the fireflies. A reasoned choice that addresses this is accepted.
s: Part (a): rock reflects, non-luminous
Part (b): light pollution and excessive tourism
Part (d): reasoned choice weighing income and the fireflies

questions.q:
A school hall has 30 traditional lamps of 60 W each. The principal plans to replace all of them with 30 LED lamps of 12 W each, costing Rs 250 per lamp, for the same brightness. The hall is lit for 5 hours a day on 200 days a year and electricity costs Rs 8 per unit (1 unit = 1 kWh = 1 kW used for 1 hour).
(a) Which feature of LED lamps from the chapter does the 60 W and 12 W comparison show?
(b) How many units of electricity does the school save in a year, and how much money?
(c) The cost of buying the LED lamps is Rs 7,500. After how many school days of lighting would the savings repay it? Does ignoring that LED lamps also last longer make this repayment time look shorter or longer than it truly is?
(d) Advise the principal on the purchase, and say what must be done when these lamps fail.
questions.a: (a) LED lamps consume much less power. (b) Power saved = 30 x 48 W = 1,440 W = 1.44 kW; 1.44 x 5 x 200 = 1,440 units; 1,440 x Rs 8 = Rs 11,520. (c) 7,500 / 11,520 x 200 = about 130 school days. Ignoring that LED lamps last longer makes it look longer than it truly is, since traditional lamps would also have to be bought again. (d) Buy the LED lamps: they repay their cost in about 130 school days, and are brighter and better for the environment. When they fail, they must be disposed of or recycled and not thrown in the garbage.
s: Part (a): much less power
Part (b): 1,440 units and Rs 11,520
Part (c): about 130 days; real repayment is shorter, so the estimate looks longer
Part (d): buy, with disposal or recycling duty

questions.q: Keshav's bus is travelling through the hills on a moonlit night. He sees the Moon over the ridge, the beams of headlight lamps of passing vehicles, the grey road lit by those beams, flashing fireflies and a distant flash of lightning. Sort all five things into those that emit their own light and those that do not, name for each luminous one whether it is natural or artificial, and say what would happen to the road if the vehicles' headlamps were switched off.
questions.a: Own light: headlight lamps (artificial), fireflies (natural, an animal), lightning (natural). Not own light: the Moon, which only reflects sunlight, and the road, which only reflects the headlight beams. If the headlamps were switched off, the road would no longer be lit by those beams and would be seen only faintly by moonlight, which is itself reflected sunlight.
s: Headlight lamps as luminous and artificial
Fireflies and lightning as luminous and natural
Moon as non-luminous, reflecting sunlight
Road as non-luminous, seen by reflected light
Switching off the headlamps removes the light the road was reflecting

questions.q: A forest where fireflies danced every summer now has far fewer. Name the three changes the chapter lists as causes, and for each suggest one step a village could take to reduce it.
questions.a: Light pollution: switch off or shield bright lights near the forest. Reduced forest cover: stop clearing trees and plant more. Excessive tourism: limit the number of visitors at a time.
s: Light pollution with a step
Reduced forest cover with a step
Excessive tourism with a step

questions.q: The chapter says light can sometimes even bend around corners, which is learnt in higher grades. Meena argues, 'So the bent-pipe activity proves nothing.' Which reply fits the chapter best?
questions.a: At this level the flame is seen through a straight pipe but not a bent one, so the activity supports straight-line travel. The chapter's result for the pipe stands as observed.
o: At this level the flame is seen through a straight pipe but not a bent one, so the activity supports straight-line travel
She is right, because if light can bend around corners the flame must also be visible through the bent pipe; so the activity proves nothing
She is right, because the chapter itself says that light travels in a bent path through pipes and curved tubes
She is wrong, because the chapter says that light can never bend around a corner anywhere, even in higher grades

questions.q: True or False: A low-power laser beam sent through a beaker of clear water with no milk leaves no visible path, so we may say that light does not travel in a straight line in clear water.
questions.a: False. Without milk the beam inside the water cannot be seen, so nothing can be said about its path. With a drop of milk added the beam is easily seen and follows a straight path.
s: Verdict: False
Correction: the beam was simply invisible; with milk it is seen to be straight

questions.q: (a) A teacher wants to show that light travels in a straight line but no adult is free to supervise a candle. Which activity from the chapter can she use instead, and what does it need? (b) Does it lead to the same conclusion as the bent pipe?
questions.a: (a) The matchbox activity with a torch, three matchboxes with holes in line and a screen; no flame is needed. (b) Yes: the spot is lost when a hole is moved out of line, so light travels in a straight line.
s: Part (a): matchbox activity with a torch
Part (b): same conclusion of straight-line travel

questions.q: Suppose light could bend freely to follow any twist. (a) What would you see on looking through the bent pipe at the candle flame? (b) What would you see on the screen when one matchbox hole is moved out of line? Say what the actual results tell us.
questions.a: (a) The flame would still be seen. (b) The spot would still appear. In the activities the flame is not seen through the bent pipe and the spot is lost when a hole is moved, so light does not bend freely; it travels in a straight line.
s: Part (a): flame would be seen
Part (b): spot would appear; actual results show straight-line travel

questions.q:
A group has 20 minutes. Test 1 uses the matchboxes and has four trials of 3 minutes each. Trial A: all three holes in line at the lamp height, screen 30 cm away. Trial B: as A but the middle box raised by 2 cm. Trial C: as A but the screen at 60 cm. Trial D: as A but the torch lamp raised 2 cm above the hole height. Test 2 uses a candle with a straight and a bent pipe, needs an adult and takes 6 minutes. The adult is free only for the first 10 minutes.
(a) Predict Trial C and say what it shows.
(b) Predict Trial B and give the reason.
(c) Predict Trial D and give the reason.
(d) In which order should the group do the two tests so that both fit? Show the timing.
questions.a: (a) The spot is still seen, because the screen is still on the straight line through the holes. (b) No spot, because the raised hole is out of line and light travels straight. (c) No spot, because the lamp, now above the hole height, no longer lies on one straight line with the holes. (d) Test 2 first (0 to 6 minutes, within the adult's 10 minutes), then Test 1 (6 to 18 minutes), a total of 18 minutes, which fits in 20; the other order would start Test 2 at 12 minutes when the adult has left.
s: Part (a): spot still seen on the line
Part (b): no spot, hole out of line
Part (c): no spot, lamp not in line
Part (d): Test 2 first with timing 6 + 12 = 18 minutes

questions.q: Mohan makes a rigid pipe in the shape of the letter Z from dull black cardboard, with a lighted candle (an adult is present) at one end. He looks into the other end in a dark room. What does he observe, and why?
questions.a: He does not see the flame, because light travels in a straight line and cannot follow the turns. A flame is seen through a straight pipe but not through a bent one.
o: He does not see the flame, because light travels in a straight line and cannot follow the turns
He sees the flame clearly, because light bends to follow the pipe through each of its turns
He sees the flame dimly, because the pipe turns its dull black walls into mirrors for the light
He sees the flame only if the pipe is also lit from the outside by a second candle

questions.q: Aman says one activity is enough to prove that light travels in a straight line. Prisha says two or three different tests are better. Whose view do you support? Use the evidence of the chapter, name a third test, and give its precautions.
questions.a: Prisha: the chapter itself uses more than one test. Test 1: three matchboxes, spot lost if a hole is out of line. Test 2: flame seen through a straight pipe but not a bent one. A third test: laser beam in water with a drop of milk, which shows a straight beam. Precautions: low-power laser, only under teacher's supervision, never at anyone's eyes.
s: Supports Prisha with the chapter's practice
Matchbox evidence
Pipe evidence
Third test: laser in milky water
Laser precautions

questions.q:
A teacher gives three kits. Kit P: three matchboxes, a torch and a screen. Kit Q: a long flexible pipe and a candle (needs an adult). Kit R: a low-power laser and milky water in a beaker (needs the teacher). Only one adult is available, who can supervise one kit at a time, and Kit P needs no supervision.
(a) For P and Q, what result shows that light travels straight?
(b) Which kit shows the path of the light directly, and which ones only show it by what is lost when something is moved or bent?
(c) State the safety rule for the kit that uses a laser.
(d) Which two kits should run at the same time, and why? Name the trade-off.
questions.a: (a) P: the spot is lost when a hole is moved out of line. Q: the flame is seen through the straight pipe but not the bent one. (b) Kit R shows the path directly as a straight beam in the milky water; P and Q show it by loss of the spot or flame. (c) Use a low-power laser only under teacher's supervision and never point the beam at anyone's eyes. (d) P can run with either Q or R, since P needs no supervision; Q and R cannot run together as they both need the one adult. Choosing R with P shows the path directly but uses the teacher's time on a laser; choosing Q with P is also acceptable if reasoned.
s: Part (a): spot lost for P; flame not seen when bent for Q
Part (b): R shows the path directly; P and Q by loss
Part (c): low-power, supervised, never at eyes
Part (d): P with Q or R, not Q with R, with a trade-off

questions.q: Divya passes a laser beam through a beaker of clear water and sees only a bright spot on the far side. She concludes that she cannot say how the light travelled inside the water. What should she add to see the path, and what will she find?
questions.a: A drop of milk; the beam inside the water follows a straight path. The drop of milk makes the beam easily visible, and it follows a straight path.
o: A drop of milk; the beam inside the water follows a straight path
A drop of ink; the beam inside the water follows a curved path
A few pieces of tracing paper; the beam inside the water stops
A mirror in the beaker; the beam inside the water splits into two

questions.q: Neha reports a bright spot on the screen although the torch lamp and the first two holes are at 4 cm above the table and the third hole is at 6 cm. Show why this result cannot happen if light travels in a straight line.
questions.a: A beam from the lamp at 4 cm through two holes at 4 cm travels straight and horizontally at 4 cm. The third hole is at 6 cm, so the beam hits the box wall and is blocked; no spot can appear. The report must be wrong.
s: Straight beam stays at 4 cm height
Third hole at 6 cm is off the line
Beam blocked, so a spot is impossible

questions.q: Imran says, 'The laser test shows light travels straight only inside water. In air we cannot say.' Do you agree? Use the tests of the chapter.
questions.a: No. The matchbox test and the bent-pipe test were done in air, and in both light behaves as if it travels in a straight line. The laser test in water is only a third test, so the conclusion holds in air as well as in water.
s: Verdict: disagrees
Matchbox test is in air and shows straight-line travel
Pipe test is in air; laser in water is one more test

questions.q: Anil bends a flexible pipe into a U shape and cannot see the candle flame (an adult is present). (a) Without moving the candle or his eye, what can he do to see the flame? (b) Why does that work?
questions.a: (a) Straighten the pipe. (b) The flame is seen along a straight pipe because light travels in a straight line from the flame to his eye.
s: Part (a): straighten the pipe
Part (b): light travels in a straight line

questions.q: You have four cardboard sheets with a hole in each, a torch, a screen and a dark room, and you must also make sure that a doubtful friend cannot say 'it was luck'. Plan the test: how you arrange the sheets, what you expect with the holes in line, what you do next to the result, what happens when you undo it, and what you conclude.
questions.a: Fix the four sheets in a row with holes at one height and in a line with the torch lamp, with the screen behind. With the holes in line a bright spot appears. Slide one sheet sideways and the spot is lost. Slide it back and the spot returns, so it was not luck. Conclusion: light travels in a straight line.
s: Arrangement with holes in line and torch at hole height
Expected bright spot when aligned
Spot lost when one sheet is moved
Spot returns when it is moved back
Conclusion of straight-line travel

questions.q: Rahul's first and third matchboxes have their holes 5 cm above the table and exactly in line with the torch lamp. The middle box has been slid 2 cm sideways, so its hole is 2 cm off that line (still 5 cm high). No spot appears on the screen. Which single action gives the spot?
questions.a: Slide the middle box back so its hole is in line with the other two. No position of the torch or screen can put a straight line through three holes when one is off the line of the other two.
o: Slide the middle box back so its hole is in line with the other two
Move the torch 2 cm sideways so that it points straight at the middle hole
Move the screen 2 cm sideways so that it lies behind the middle hole
Darken the room further and wait for the spot to show up

questions.q: Rohit stands behind the third matchbox and looks back through the three holes towards the torch lamp. (a) He sees the lamp. What can he say about the three holes and the lamp? (b) He then sees nothing at all, although the lamp is on. What does that tell him?
questions.a: (a) The holes and the lamp lie on one straight line. (b) They are not all on one line: at least one box has been moved out of line, or the lamp is not at the height of the holes.
s: Part (a): holes and lamp on one straight line
Part (b): at least one is out of line

questions.q:
Assertion (A): If a bright spot is obtained on the screen in the matchbox activity, the three holes must lie in one straight line.
Reason (R): Light travels in a straight line.
questions.a: Both A and R are true and R explains A. Light can reach the screen only by travelling straight through the holes, so the spot tells us the holes are in one line.
o: Both A and R are true and R explains A
Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true

questions.q: In a matchbox set-up the torch lamp, the three holes and the screen are all at the same height, yet there is no spot on the screen. Give two different faults, not about height, that could explain it, and say how you would check each.
questions.a: Fault 1: one box has slid sideways, so its hole is off the line; check by looking along the row and sliding it back. Fault 2: the torch is pointing away from the first hole or is off the line; check by turning the torch so that its lamp points through the holes.
s: First fault, not about height
Second fault, not about height
A way to check each

questions.q: Zara's three matchboxes have holes at the same height, except that she punches the middle hole 1 cm lower. The torch lamp is at the height of the other holes. Hoping to find the spot, she slides the screen sideways and back and forth. What happens?
questions.a: No spot appears anywhere, because the middle hole blocks the beam. Light travels in a straight line, so a hole out of line blocks the beam whatever the screen position.
o: No spot appears anywhere, because the middle hole blocks the beam
The spot appears when the screen is moved far enough to one side of the boxes
The spot appears on the screen but is fainter than before, since less light passes through
The spot appears only if the screen is moved closer to the boxes and the room is dark

questions.q: Four students propose a test to check that light travels in a straight line. Which test is the best design?
questions.a: Get the spot with three aligned holes, then shift one hole sideways and see if it is lost. Comparing the aligned and shifted arrangements is a fair test; the others have no comparison or test something else.
o: Get the spot with three aligned holes, then shift one hole sideways and see if it is lost
Switch the torch on in a bright room and compare how bright the wall looks at noon and at night
Look at a candle flame through a straight pipe only, and never try a bent one to compare
Shine the torch into a mirror and note where the spot falls on the wall in different positions

questions.q:
Statement 1: Seeing a candle flame through a straight pipe but not through the same pipe bent shows that the shape of the path matters for light.
Statement 2: A bright spot on the screen in the matchbox activity shows that light has gone through all three holes along a straight path.
Statement 3: A straight laser beam in milky water proves that light never changes direction under any circumstances.
Which statements are correct?
questions.a: 1 and 2 only. The pipe and matchbox results fit straight-line travel; but light does change direction at a mirror, so a straight beam in water cannot prove that it never changes direction.
o: 1 and 2 only
1 and 3 only
2 and 3 only
1, 2 and 3

questions.q: (a) A clear glass sheet is held between a torch and a screen. Will it be said that there is no shadow at all? (b) Compare, with a reason, the expected shadows of the glass sheet and of a tracing-paper sheet.
questions.a: (a) No: some transparent objects can make a faint shadow. (b) The glass shadow is fainter, because glass lets light pass almost completely, while tracing paper lets light pass only partly and blocks more, giving a lighter shadow.
s: Part (a): possibly a faint shadow, not none
Part (b): glass fainter than tracing paper, with reason

questions.q: Four students try to change the shadow of a card held between a fixed torch and a fixed screen. Pia paints the card red. Joy tilts the card. Kim moves the card nearer to the torch. Lal moves the card nearer to the screen. Whose change will leave the shape and size of the shadow unaltered?
questions.a: Pia's. The colour of an opaque object does not change its shadow, but tilting it or moving it nearer the torch or the screen changes the position of the object relative to the light source and the screen, and so changes the shadow.
o: Pia's
Joy's
Kim's
Lal's

questions.q: In Activity 11.4 a ball stands between a lit torch and a screen and casts a shadow. When only the ball is removed, keeping the torch and the screen as they were, the screen shows a bright ___.
questions.a: spot

questions.q:
Assertion (A): The shadow of a brightly coloured kite on the ground looks dark, not coloured like the kite.
Reason (R): A shadow is the dark patch where an opaque object has blocked light from reaching the screen.
questions.a: Both A and R are true and R explains A. The shadow is where light is blocked, so it is dark whatever the colour of the object.
o: Both A and R are true and R explains A
Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true

questions.q: A puppeteer wants the shadow of a flat puppet to look bigger on the screen. The lamp and the screen cannot be moved. What should she do?
questions.a: Hold the puppet nearer to the lamp. The size of a shadow depends on the position of the object relative to the light source and the screen; moving the object closer to the source makes the shadow larger.
o: Hold the puppet nearer to the lamp
Hold the puppet nearer to the screen
Paint the puppet a darker colour
Replace the puppet with a tracing-paper cut-out of the same shape

questions.q: In a large dark hall Rina holds a book in front of a lit torch. The beam passes over empty space and there is no surface behind the book, so she sees no shadow anywhere. What should she do?
questions.a: Place a screen such as a cardboard behind the book, in the beam's path. A shadow needs a source of light, an opaque object and a screen on which to see it.
o: Place a screen such as a cardboard behind the book, in the beam's path
Switch off the torch so that the book can be seen more easily in the dark hall
Replace the book with a sheet of clear glass so that the light passes through it
Paint the book a darker colour so that its shadow becomes visible

questions.q: A ball stands between a torch and a wall. Predict what the wall shows in each of these changes, giving the reason: (i) the ball is moved nearer to the torch; (ii) a second identical torch is switched on a few centimetres from the first; (iii) the ball is taken away; (iv) the torch is switched off with the ball in place.
questions.a: (i) The shadow becomes larger, because its size depends on the position of the ball relative to the torch and the wall. (ii) Two shadows appear, one for each torch. (iii) A bright spot of torch light appears with no shadow, because nothing blocks the light. (iv) No shadow and no spot, because without a source of light there is nothing to be blocked.
s: (i) larger shadow with reason of position
(ii) two shadows, one for each torch
(iii) bright spot, nothing blocks the light
(iv) no light, so no shadow
Links each answer to the needs and the position of source, object, screen

questions.q:
Ananya tests four sheets P, Q, R and S one at a time between a torch and a screen. With P, no light reaches the screen. With Q, a dim patch of light reaches it. With R, almost all the light reaches the screen. With S, only a very faint glow reaches it, fainter than with Q. The school wants a window blind for a hall that hides what is inside but still lets in some daylight.
(a) Classify P, Q, R and S.
(b) Q is cut into a flat figure and P into the same figure, and each is held in the same place before the torch. How do the two shadows compare?
(c) Is it possible that R forms any shadow at all? Explain.
(d) Which sheet would you choose for the blind, Q or S, and what do you give up?
questions.a: (a) P opaque; Q and S translucent; R transparent. (b) Q's shadow is lighter than P's, because Q lets some light through while P blocks all of it. (c) Possibly a faint one, because the chapter says that some transparent objects can create faint shadows. (d) Q lets in more daylight but hides less; S hides more but makes the hall dimmer. Either is accepted if the trade-off is stated; P would block all light and R would not hide the room.
s: Part (a): classification of all four
Part (b): lighter shadow for Q than for P, with reason
Part (c): possibly a faint shadow from some transparent objects
Part (d): choice with the trade-off

questions.q: We do not see the shadow of a bird flying high in the sky, but we see it on the ground when the bird swoops down low. (a) Which of the three needs for a shadow is present in both cases? (b) Using the chapter's statement on shadows, explain the difference.
questions.a: (a) All three: the Sun as the source, the bird as the opaque object and the ground as the screen. (b) The shape, size and sharpness of a shadow depend on the position of the object relative to the source and the screen, so the shadow of the high bird is not sharp enough to be seen while that of the low bird is.
s: Part (a): source, object and screen are all present
Part (b): sharpness depends on position of the object

questions.q: A square card is held facing a torch and its shadow on a screen is a square. (a) Predict what can happen to the shape of the shadow if the card is tilted, with the torch and screen fixed. (b) Why can a shadow alone not always tell you what the object looks like?
questions.a: (a) The shape of the shadow changes and may no longer be a square. (b) Shape, size and sharpness of a shadow depend on the position of the object relative to the light source and the screen, so the shadow may not look like the object.
s: Part (a): shape of shadow changes on tilting
Part (b): shadow depends on position, so it may not match the object

questions.q: A student sees only an evenly bright spot of torch light on the screen and no dark patch at all. Give two different explanations consistent with the activity and say how to check each.
questions.a: (1) No object is in the path of the light; put an opaque object between the torch and screen and a dark patch appears. (2) The object in the path is transparent (or nearly), which forms at most a faint shadow; replace it with an opaque object to see a dark shadow.
s: First explanation (nothing in the path)
Second explanation (transparent object)
A way to check each

questions.q: A ball stands in front of a wall. Two identical torches, a few centimetres apart, shine on it from its left; both are switched on, and the ball is far enough from the wall that its patches do not overlap. What does the wall show?
questions.a: Two dark patches, because the ball blocks each torch's light separately. Each torch gives its own shadow.
o: Two dark patches, because the ball blocks each torch's light separately
One dark patch, because a ball can block only one beam of light at a time
One very dark patch, because two torches together give a darker shadow than one torch
No dark patch at all, because two beams of light cancel each other on the wall

questions.q: Meena says, 'To get a dark shadow of my hand on a wall I need a lit lamp, my hand and the wall; and if I wear a red glove the shadow will not turn red.' Do you agree? Explain.
questions.a: Yes. A shadow needs a source of light, an opaque object (the hand) and a screen (the wall). The colour of an opaque object does not change the colour of its shadow, so the red glove makes no difference.
s: Verdict: agrees
Names source, opaque object and screen
Colour of the opaque object does not change the shadow

questions.q: Ishaan wants to find out whether the colour of an opaque cut-out changes the colour of its shadow, and whether the position of the lamp matters. Plan the experiment: what he changes, what he keeps the same, what he expects to observe, and the conclusions.
questions.a: He uses one lamp, one screen and two cut-outs of the same shape, one red and one green, keeping lamp and screen fixed and changing only the colour. Expected: both shadows are the same dark patch, so colour of an opaque object does not change its shadow's colour. Then he moves the lamp or the cut-out and notes that shape, size and sharpness of the shadow change with the positions of object, source and screen. Conclusions: colour has no effect; position does.
s: Colour is the one thing changed, other things fixed
Expected result: same dark shadow
Second test: moves lamp or object
Observes size, shape or sharpness change
States both conclusions

questions.q: A pole stands on level ground. Its shadow, measured in the morning, at noon and in the evening, has three different lengths. (a) The pole and the ground did not move; which one of the three things needed for a shadow changed? (b) Which statement of the chapter explains why the shadow changed?
questions.a: (a) The source of light, since the position of the Sun in the sky changed. (b) The shape, size and sharpness of a shadow depend on the position of the object relative to the light source and the screen.
s: Part (a): the Sun, the source of light, changed position
Part (b): shadow depends on position of object relative to source and screen

questions.q: A teacher places a wooden board, a steel plate, tracing paper and clear glass one at a time between a torch and a screen. Classify each, and arrange them from the darkest shadow to the faintest.
questions.a: Wooden board and steel plate: opaque; tracing paper: translucent; clear glass: transparent. Order: board and steel plate (darkest), then tracing paper (lighter), then clear glass (faintest).
s: Correct classification of the four
Darkest first: opaque
Translucent lighter, transparent faintest

questions.q: In a shadow play the puppeteer keeps the puppet still but slowly moves the lamp. (a) What happens to the shadow on the screen? (b) Which one of the three things needed for a shadow did she move, and what does this tell you about how life-like movements are created?
questions.a: (a) The shadow moves and changes on the screen. (b) She moved the source of light; moving the light or the puppets changes the position of the object relative to the source and the screen, which creates movement.
s: Part (a): the shadow changes position or size
Part (b): source moved; puppets and light create movement

questions.q:
Match each observation in Column A with what it shows in Column B.
Column A: 1 A torch spot looks dim but visible behind a sheet  2 The torch spot looks almost as bright behind a sheet, with at most a faint shadow  3 No light spot at all behind the sheet, only a dark patch  4 An opaque card stands in front of the screen but the torch is off
Column B: a Opaque sheet  b Transparent sheet  c Translucent sheet  d No shadow because no light falls on the card
questions.a: 1-c, 2-b, 3-a, 4-d. A dim spot means translucent, an almost bright spot means transparent, a dark patch with no light means opaque, and with the torch off there is no light to be blocked.

questions.q:
Statement 1: To see a shadow we need a source of light, an opaque object and a surface that acts as a screen.
Statement 2: With the torch and the screen fixed, moving an opaque object closer to the torch can change the size of its shadow.
Statement 3: A translucent sheet and an opaque sheet of the same size always make shadows of the same darkness.
Which statements are correct?
questions.a: 1 and 2 only. The three needs and the effect of position come from the activity; an opaque sheet makes a darker shadow than a translucent one, so Statement 3 is false.
o: 1 and 2 only
1 and 3 only
2 and 3 only
1, 2 and 3

questions.q:
A shadow-puppet troupe uses one lamp and a cloth screen. The hero is a flat card figure, the ghost is cut from a thin tracing sheet, and a spare ghost is cut from clear plastic.
(a) During the fight scene the hero figure is moved from near the screen to near the lamp. What happens to the size of its shadow?
(b) The director paints the hero's card red in one scene and green in another. What colour is the shadow in each?
(c) What kind of shadow does the ghost cut from tracing sheet give, compared with the one from clear plastic?
(d) To make the screen brighter, a helper wants to add a second lamp beside the first. What would this do to each figure's shadow, and would you allow it?
questions.a: (a) The shadow becomes larger, since its size depends on the position of the figure relative to the lamp and the screen. (b) The same dark shadow in both scenes, since the colour of an opaque object does not change the colour of its shadow. (c) Tracing sheet: a lighter shadow; clear plastic: at most a faint shadow. (d) Each figure would get two shadows, one for each lamp, which can confuse the audience; a reasoned choice (refuse, or accept for a special effect) is acceptable.
s: Part (a): shadow larger when the figure is nearer the lamp
Part (b): same dark shadow in both colours
Part (c): lighter versus faint
Part (d): two shadows per figure, with a reasoned decision

questions.q: True or False: When a plane mirror is tilted slightly in steady sunlight, the spot of reflected light on the wall moves, even though the light reaching the mirror has not changed.
questions.a: True. The mirror changes the direction of the light that falls on it; tilting the mirror changes the new direction, so the spot lands at a different place.
s: Verdict: True
Reason: the direction of reflected light depends on how the mirror is tilted

questions.q: Kabir throws a steady spot of sunlight on a wall using a steel plate. A friend now holds a large dark cloth between the Sun and the plate, so that no sunlight falls on the plate. What happens to the spot on the wall, and why?
questions.a: It disappears, as no light falls on the plate for it to redirect. A reflecting surface only changes the direction of light that falls on it.
o: It disappears, as no light falls on the plate for it to redirect
It stays, because the plate produces light of its own all the time
It turns dark, because the cloth makes a shadow in its place on the wall
It moves higher, because the cloth tilts the plate as it is held up

questions.q:
The village library has a reading corner whose wall never gets direct sunlight. Rohan places a plane mirror on the window ledge and gets a spot of reflected sunlight in the corner at 10 a.m. By 11 a.m. the spot has slid off the corner, although the mirror has not been touched. Plan P: leave the mirror fixed all day. Plan Q: a volunteer re-tilts the mirror every half hour.
(a) What is the mirror doing to the sunlight to put a spot on the shaded wall?
(b) The spot is lower than the corner. What should Rohan do to the mirror to move it higher?
(c) A child says, 'The spot is the mirror's own lamp.' How can Rohan show her she is wrong?
(d) Which plan would you advise, and what does each cost or gain?
questions.a: (a) It changes the direction of the sunlight falling on it (reflection) and sends it to the wall. (b) Tilt the mirror so that it sends the light higher. (c) Cover the mirror from the Sun with a card: the spot disappears, so the light came from the Sun and the mirror only redirected it. (d) Plan Q keeps the spot in the corner but needs a volunteer's time; Plan P needs no one but the spot drifts away. A reasoned choice or a combined plan is accepted.
s: Part (a): reflection of sunlight
Part (b): tilt the mirror so that it sends the light higher
Part (c): spot vanishes when sunlight is blocked, so mirror does not make light
Part (d): reasoned choice with cost and gain

questions.q: In Activity 11.6 a thin beam on white paper meets a plane mirror and changes direction. (a) What would you expect to see if Radha now tilts the mirror a little? (b) Which word names what the mirror does to the beam?
questions.a: (a) The beam leaves the mirror along another new direction, so its path on the paper changes. (b) Reflection.
s: Part (a): the path of the beam changes again
Part (b): reflection

questions.q: In Activity 11.6 Radha's torch shines through a comb and she sees a wide, fuzzy band of light on the white paper instead of a thin beam. Which change follows the activity to get the thin beam she needs before placing the mirror?
questions.a: Cover all openings of the comb with black paper except one. Closing all openings but one makes a thin slit, which gives a thin beam.
o: Cover all openings of the comb with black paper except one
Remove the white paper so that the band of light can spread out
Place the mirror before the comb so that it cleans the beam
Switch the torch off and on again several times to steady the beam

questions.q:
Four trekkers on a hillside want to signal to a camp 100 m away across a valley, using a small plane mirror. The Sun is hidden by cloud for the next 20 minutes of the 30 minutes they can wait.
(a) Why would a dull black cloth be useless for the signal?
(b) When the Sun comes out, the flash lands on a rock beside the camp, not on the camp. What should they change?
(c) With the Sun still hidden, a trekker suggests shining a torch at the mirror instead. Will the mirror still send a beam to the camp? Explain.
(d) The torch battery is weak, and the Sun is likely to return in 20 minutes. Should they wait for the Sun or use the torch now? Weigh them.
questions.a: (a) A dull cloth does not change the direction of light into a flash; a shiny surface such as a mirror does. (b) Tilt (turn) the mirror so that the reflected light points at the camp. (c) Yes: the mirror changes the direction of the torch light just as it does for sunlight, as in the torch and mirror activity. (d) Using the torch now may give a dimmer flash from a weak battery but is immediate; waiting for the Sun gives a brighter flash but uses 20 of the 30 minutes. A reasoned decision is accepted.
s: Part (a): a dull cloth does not reflect; a shiny surface does
Part (b): tilt the mirror to aim the flash
Part (c): mirror redirects torch light too
Part (d): reasoned choice weighing weak torch against waiting

questions.q: Kabir's sunlight spot is on the wall near the floor. He wants it higher on the same wall, and neither he nor the Sun may move. What should he do with the steel plate?
questions.a: Tilt the plate so that it sends the light higher. Tilting changes the direction of the reflected light and so the position of the spot.
o: Tilt the plate so that it sends the light higher
Hold the plate nearer to his face and look into it
Paint the plate a lighter colour so that the spot is bright
Cover half the plate with a black paper to cut the light

questions.q: A spot of sunlight sent by a mirror falls on a wall. A student holds a cardboard sheet between the mirror and the wall, across the path of the reflected light. (a) Where does the spot now appear? (b) What does this show about the light after reflection?
questions.a: (a) On the cardboard (the wall no longer gets the spot). (b) After reflection the light still travels in a straight line and an opaque sheet blocks it.
s: Part (a): spot appears on the cardboard and is lost from the wall
Part (b): reflected light travels in a straight line and is blocked by an opaque object

questions.q: Rina reports that after she tilted a plane mirror noticeably, the spot of reflected sunlight on the wall stayed exactly where it was, with the Sun in the same place. Show that this cannot be right.
questions.a: A mirror changes the direction of the light that falls on it. Tilting the mirror changes the direction in which the light leaves it. Since light travels straight after the mirror, a new direction must send the light to a different place, so the spot must move. A spot that did not move contradicts this.
s: A mirror changes the direction of light
Tilting changes the direction of the reflected light
So the spot must move; a fixed spot is impossible

questions.q: (a) Before glass mirrors were made, mirrors were made by polishing stone or metal. Could such a polished metal surface be used in Activity 11.5 to put a spot of sunlight on a wall? (b) Name the property common to every mirror, glass or metal, that makes this possible.
questions.a: (a) Yes: a shiny polished metal surface redirects sunlight like a steel plate or glass mirror. (b) It changes the direction of the light falling on it (reflection).
s: Part (a): yes, a polished metal surface can do it
Part (b): it changes the direction of light (reflection)

questions.q: On a bus ride Keshav says, 'Moonlight is light of the same kind as the flash I get from my steel water bottle in the Sun.' Aryan replies, 'No, moonlight is made by the Moon itself.' Which is correct?
questions.a: Keshav, since both are sunlight whose direction was changed by the Moon and the bottle. The Moon is non-luminous; it reflects the sunlight that falls on it.
o: Keshav, since both are sunlight whose direction was changed by the Moon and the bottle
Aryan, because the Moon is a very big object and so makes its own light
Keshav, but only because the bottle and the Moon are both luminous objects
Aryan, because only artificial objects like bottles can reflect sunlight

questions.q: A bright spot is seen on a wall that gets no direct sunlight and no lamp is on. Give two different arrangements that could cause this, and say what they have in common.
questions.a: A shiny steel plate held in sunlight and turned towards the wall; a plane mirror held in sunlight and turned towards the wall. In both, a shiny surface changes the direction of the sunlight falling on it (reflection) and sends it to the wall.
s: First arrangement (e.g. steel plate)
Second arrangement (e.g. plane mirror)
Common idea: a shiny surface changes the direction of light

questions.q: Imran shines a torch beam in turn on a polished steel plate and on a dull black cloth, in a dark room, hoping to put a bright spot on a second wall at the side. Which gives that bright spot, and why?
questions.a: The polished steel plate, because a shiny surface changes the direction of light. A shiny surface or mirror changes the direction of light falling on it, which is reflection.
o: The polished steel plate, because a shiny surface changes the direction of light
The black cloth, because it takes in the light and then sends it on to the side wall
Both, because every object changes the direction of any light that falls on it
Neither, because a torch beam can only make a shadow and never a spot of light

questions.q:
Statement 1: A plane mirror held in sunlight can send a bright spot to a wall that the Sun does not reach directly.
Statement 2: The spot on the wall is bright because the mirror itself makes extra light.
Statement 3: Tilting the mirror changes where the spot falls, while light still travels in straight lines on each side of the mirror.
Which statements are correct?
questions.a: 1 and 3 only. The mirror only changes the direction of the sunlight falling on it (reflection); it does not make extra light, so Statement 2 is false.
o: 1 and 3 only
1 and 2 only
2 and 3 only
1, 2 and 3

questions.q: Plan an investigation into how the position of a sunlight spot on a wall depends on the tilt of a plane mirror. Say what you will keep fixed, what you will change, what you will observe, what you conclude about the path of light, and one thing you will compare with a shadow experiment.
questions.a: Keep the Sun side, the wall and the mirror's place fixed; change only the tilt of the mirror, a little at a time. Observe that the spot moves to a new position for each tilt. Conclusion: the mirror changes the direction of light (reflection) while light still travels in straight lines. Comparison: in a shadow the object blocks light, but here the mirror sends the light on in a new direction.
s: Keeps place of mirror and wall fixed
Changes only the tilt
Observes the spot moving
Concludes reflection and straight-line paths
Valid contrast with a shadow

questions.q: In Activity 11.5 a shiny steel plate in sunlight made a shadow on the screen and also a bright spot on the opposite wall. (a) Which of the two results comes from the plate blocking light? (b) Which comes from the plate changing the direction of light? Explain both.
questions.a: (a) The shadow: the opaque plate blocks light from reaching the screen. (b) The bright spot: the shiny surface sends the light that falls on it in a new direction towards the wall (reflection).
s: Part (a): shadow from blocked light
Part (b): bright spot from reflection

questions.q:
Assertion (A): In a room with absolutely no light, a person cannot see her own face in a plane mirror.
Reason (R): A plane mirror does not give out light of its own; it only changes the direction of light falling on it.
questions.a: Both A and R are true and R explains A. With no light there is nothing for the mirror to redirect to her eyes, and the mirror supplies none of its own.
o: Both A and R are true and R explains A
Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true

questions.q: Priya watches a thin beam on white paper hit a plane mirror and leave it in a new direction. She says, 'So light does not really travel in straight lines; it bends in a curve at the mirror.' What is the best reply?
questions.a: Light still travels in straight lines before and after the mirror; only its direction changes at the mirror. The chapter says light always travels in straight lines and changes direction when it falls on a shiny surface.
o: Light still travels in straight lines before and after the mirror; only its direction changes at the mirror
She is right, because the beam has a different direction after the mirror than before it, so it must curve
She is right, because a mirror makes light travel in curves wherever it falls on a shiny surface
She is wrong, because light goes straight through a mirror without changing its direction at all

questions.q: Rekha's father runs a roadside shop whose signboard stays in shade the whole day while the shop opposite is in sunlight. Suggest how a flat shiny steel sheet or plane mirror could be used to light the signboard, what to do if the spot drifts off the board, and what stays true about the light's path.
questions.a: Place the sheet or mirror in the sunlight and turn it so the sunlight is directed on to the signboard. If the spot drifts off the board, tilt the sheet to move it back. Light still travels in straight lines to the sheet and from it; only its direction is changed by reflection. A shiny flat surface is needed.
s: Uses sunlight on a shiny flat surface
Turns it to direct light on to the board
Tilts to bring the spot back onto the board
Light still travels in straight lines
Reflection changes only the direction

questions.q: Kabir wants to send a bright flash of sunlight to a friend standing at the far end of the school ground, using a shiny steel plate. Describe how he should use the plate, what he should do if the flash falls short of his friend, and what his friend would see.
questions.a: He holds the plate in sunlight and turns it so the reflected light travels towards his friend. If the flash falls short he tilts the plate to change the position of the spot. His friend sees a bright spot of light, because the plate has changed the direction of sunlight (reflection).
s: Turns the plate to direct sunlight at his friend
Tilts it to adjust the spot
Reflection explains the flash

questions.q: Tarun says, 'The sunlight spot on the wall comes from the steel plate itself, so the plate is a luminous object.' Do you agree? Explain.
questions.a: No. The plate only changes the direction of sunlight falling on it (reflection); it does not emit its own light. So it is non-luminous.
s: Verdict: disagree
Plate redirects sunlight, i.e. reflection
Does not emit its own light, hence non-luminous

questions.q: Rohit stands in front of a plane mirror and sees his image behind it. He holds a white card exactly where the image seems to be, behind the mirror, and then holds another card in front of the mirror. On which card will he see a picture of himself?
questions.a: On neither card, because a plane mirror image cannot be obtained on a screen. The chapter says this holds whether the screen is behind or in front of the mirror.
o: On neither card, because a plane mirror image cannot be obtained on a screen
On the card behind the mirror, because the image seems to be located there
On the card in front of the mirror, because the light from his face falls there
On both cards, but only if the room is dark enough

questions.q: Leela claims that she caught the image of a candle flame on a white card held behind a plane mirror and that it was sharp. Show that this claim cannot be correct.
questions.a: The chapter states that the image formed by a plane mirror cannot be obtained on a screen. A white card is a screen, wherever it is placed behind or in front of the mirror. So a sharp picture on the card is impossible; Leela's claim must be wrong.
s: States that the plane mirror image cannot be obtained on a screen
A white card is a screen, behind or in front
So the claimed result is impossible

questions.q: Rohit moves a white screen all around behind a plane mirror and then in front of it, and never gets a picture on it. (a) What does he conclude about the image? (b) How is it that he can still see the image when he looks into the mirror?
questions.a: (a) The image of a plane mirror cannot be obtained on a screen. (b) He sees it by looking into the mirror: it appears to be behind the mirror, but it is not a picture formed on a surface.
s: Part (a): the image cannot be obtained on a screen
Part (b): seen by looking into the mirror, appears behind it, not caught on a surface

questions.q: Kavya says, 'When I walk away from a plane mirror my image stays the same size, and it stays at the same place behind the mirror.' Do you agree? Explain.
questions.a: Partly. The size claim is right: the image is the same size as the object at every position. The second claim is wrong: when she stands far from the mirror the image appears far from the mirror too, so it appears farther behind the mirror as she walks away.
s: Verdict: partly agrees (size right, place wrong)
Same size at every position
Image appears farther as she moves away

questions.q: A class hangs four cards facing a large plane mirror: TOOT, TOTO, OTT and TTO. (T and O look identical to themselves in a plane mirror.) Write what the image of each card reads, say which card or cards read the same in the mirror as they do directly, and say which two cards form a pair whose images are each other's directly read form.
questions.a: TOOT reads TOOT; TOTO reads OTOT; OTT reads TTO; TTO reads OTT. TOOT reads the same in the mirror as directly. OTT and TTO form a pair: the image of each reads like the other card.
s: Image of TOOT: TOOT
Image of TOTO: OTOT
Images of OTT and TTO: TTO and OTT
Only TOOT reads the same in the mirror and directly
OTT and TTO form the pair, by lateral inversion reversing the order

questions.q: Daniel writes his name on a sheet of paper and holds it up, parallel to a plane mirror. (a) How does the image of his name differ from the writing on the sheet? (b) Is the image of his name upside down? Give the reason.
questions.a: (a) The left and right of the writing are interchanged (lateral inversion). (b) No: the image of a plane mirror is erect, so only left and right change.
s: Part (a): lateral inversion
Part (b): erect, not upside down

questions.q: T and O each look identical to themselves in a plane mirror. A prop card must show OTT when it is looked at in a plane mirror. What should be written on the card itself?
questions.a: TTO. Lateral inversion reverses the order of the letters, so the card must read the reverse of OTT.
o: TTO
OTT
TOT
OOT

questions.q:
In a dance class Kavya stands 1.2 m in front of a large plane mirror, holding a red ribbon in her left hand. She raises that hand. She then steps back 0.8 m from where she stood. A dancer says, 'When I step back my image looks smaller, so I cannot check my pose.' The teacher wants dancers to check a move called 'left arm up' using the mirror.
(a) Which arm does her image raise, and in which hand of the image is the ribbon?
(b) How far is she from the mirror after stepping back, and how does her image appear compared with before?
(c) Is the dancer's complaint correct? Explain.
(d) Should the dancers use the mirror to check 'left arm up'? Decide and say what they must keep in mind.
questions.a: (a) The right arm of the image, and the ribbon is in the image's right hand, by lateral inversion. (b) 1.2 + 0.8 = 2.0 m; the image appears farther from the mirror than before, because she stands farther, but it is the same size. (c) No: the plane mirror image is the same size as the object at every position. (d) Yes, if they remember lateral inversion: the left arm they raise appears as the right arm of the image, so they should expect the image's right arm; a reasoned 'no' that suggests checking by a classmate instead is also accepted.
s: Part (a): right arm and ribbon in the right hand of the image
Part (b): 2.0 m; image appears farther, same size
Part (c): complaint wrong, same size
Part (d): decision using lateral inversion

questions.q: A garage owner wants to paint FIRE SERVICE on his van so that a driver ahead reads it correctly in the rear-view mirror. (a) How should the letters be painted? (b) A helper says to paint them upside down as well. Why is that wrong?
questions.a: (a) Laterally inverted (left and right interchanged), so that the mirror interchanges them again and the driver reads it correctly. (b) A plane mirror image is erect and not upside down, so upside-down letters would appear upside down in the mirror.
s: Part (a): laterally inverted lettering
Part (b): the mirror image is not upside down, so no upside-down painting

questions.q:
Match each observation in Column A with the property of a plane mirror image that it shows in Column B.
Column A: 1 She raises her left arm and her image raises its right  2 A white card moved all around behind the mirror shows no picture  3 A pen's tip stays on top wherever the pen is placed  4 As she steps back, the image seems to move back too
Column B: a Erect image  b Cannot be obtained on a screen  c Lateral inversion  d Appears far when the object stands far
questions.a: 1-c, 2-b, 3-a, 4-d. Left-right swap is lateral inversion, no picture on a card means no screen image, the tip on top means erect, and an image that moves back with the object appears far when the object stands far.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): When the word AMBULANCE painted on a vehicle is read in a plane mirror, it appears upside down.
Reason (R): The image formed by a plane mirror is laterally inverted.
questions.a: A is false but R is true. A plane mirror image is laterally inverted but it is erect, not upside down, so Assertion A is false.
o: A is false but R is true
Both A and R are true and R explains A
Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
A is true but R is false

questions.q: Nina stands 1 m from a large plane mirror and Ishan, a boy of the same height, stands 4 m from it. Each looks at his or her own image. Which statement fits the chapter?
questions.a: Ishan's image appears farther from the mirror than Nina's, and each image is as big as its owner. The image appears close when you stand close and far when you stand far, and it is the same size as the object.
o: Ishan's image appears farther from the mirror than Nina's, and each image is as big as its owner
Ishan's image appears at the same distance from the mirror as Nina's, but it is smaller since he stands farther away
Ishan's image appears closer to the mirror than Nina's, and it is smaller since he is farther away
Nina's image appears larger than Ishan's, because she stands closer to the mirror and the image grows

questions.q: A manager says, 'To make a lorry's front word readable in the mirror of the car ahead, paint it laterally inverted and also upside down.' Evaluate his plan: what a plane mirror does to left and right, what it does to up and down, what the driver ahead would see with his plan, and what you advise.
questions.a: A plane mirror interchanges left and right (lateral inversion). It does not turn the image upside down; the image is erect. With the manager's plan the word would read correctly left to right but appear upside down in the mirror. Advise painting only laterally inverted, like AMBULANCE on an ambulance, so it reads correctly in the rear-view mirror.
s: Mirror interchanges left and right
Mirror image is erect, not upside down
Laterally inverted lettering reads correctly in the mirror
His upside-down addition would appear upside down
Advice: only laterally inverted lettering

questions.q: Write a secret message for a friend that can be read only by holding it in front of a plane mirror. Say how you would write it and what the friend will see in the mirror.
questions.a: Write the words reversed from left to right (laterally inverted), for example write the letters in reverse order with each letter reversed. In the mirror, lateral inversion swaps left and right again, so the friend sees the message reading correctly.
s: Writes the message laterally inverted
Mirror reverses left and right again
Message appears correct in the image

questions.q: (a) Why does a T in front of a plane mirror look unchanged in the image while an R looks reversed? (b) Of OTTO and TTO, which one reads the same in a plane mirror as it does directly? (Take T and O as unchanged.)
questions.a: (a) The mirror interchanges left and right; T looks the same after the swap but R does not. (b) OTTO, because reversing the order of its letters gives OTTO again; TTO reads OTT.
s: Part (a): left and right interchanged; T unchanged, R reversed
Part (b): OTTO, since reversed it is the same

questions.q:
The school drama club will place a card at the back of the stage that actors read by looking at its image in a large plane mirror, while the audience in front can read the card directly. T and O look identical to themselves in a plane mirror. The club first uses a card with the two letters TO.
(a) How will the image of the card TO read in the mirror?
(b) Which property of the image explains this?
(c) How should the club write a card so that its image reads TO?
(d) The club wants a single card that reads correctly both directly and in the mirror. Is that possible, and for which kind of word?
questions.a: (a) The letters look identical but their order is reversed: it reads OT. (b) Lateral inversion: left and right appear interchanged. (c) Write OT, which becomes TO in the image. (d) For the card TO a single card is not possible, since it reads OT in the mirror; but a word that reads the same backwards, such as TOT or TOOT, reads the same directly and in the mirror, so one such card would work.
s: Part (a): reads OT
Part (b): lateral inversion
Part (c): write OT
Part (d): not for TO; possible for a word like TOT or TOOT

questions.q: Shabnam says, 'My image in the mirror is smaller when I stand far, because it looks small.' (a) Is her claim correct, according to the chapter? (b) Describe a simple test with a pen that checks the size of the image at different positions.
questions.a: (a) No: the image formed by a plane mirror is of the same size as the object. (b) Place the pen at several positions in front of the mirror and compare the size of its image each time; the sizes are the same.
s: Part (a): claim incorrect, image is the same size
Part (b): move the pen to different positions and compare the image sizes

questions.q:
Statement 1: The image in a plane mirror becomes smaller as the object stands farther from the mirror.
Statement 2: The image in a plane mirror is erect, but its left and right appear interchanged.
Statement 3: The image in a plane mirror cannot be caught on a screen, whether the screen is placed behind or in front of the mirror.
Which statements are correct?
questions.a: 2 and 3 only. The image is the same size as the object at every position, so Statement 1 is false; the other two follow the chapter.
o: 2 and 3 only
1 and 2 only
1 and 3 only
1, 2 and 3

questions.q: T and O each look identical to themselves in a plane mirror. Of the words TOOT, TOTO, OTTO, TTO, OTT and TOT, the number whose image in a plane mirror reads exactly the same as the word itself is ___.
Aman faces a plane mirror holding a pen in his right hand with the tip pointing up. Which description of the image is correct?
questions.a: The pen appears in the image's left hand, with the tip still pointing up. Right appears left (lateral inversion), but the image is erect, not upside down.
o: The pen appears in the image's left hand, with the tip still pointing up
The pen appears in the image's right hand, with the tip pointing down
The pen appears in the image's left hand, with the tip pointing down
The pen appears in the image's right hand, with the tip still pointing up

questions.q:
Assertion (A): If the pinhole of a pinhole camera is covered with a thick opaque card, no image of a distant bright tree forms on its screen.
Reason (R): An opaque object lets light pass through it partially.
questions.a: A is true but R is false. An opaque object does not let light pass, which is why no light reaches the screen; R is false.
o: A is true but R is false
Both A and R are true and R explains A
Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
A is false but R is true

questions.q:
Match each task in Column A with the device in Column B that suits it best.
Column A: 1 A soldier looks out of a bunker without raising his head  2 A designer wants ever-changing patterns for new designs  3 A student views a sunlit building as a picture on tracing paper  4 A child looks at her own face
Column B: a Pinhole camera  b Periscope  c Kaleidoscope  d Plane mirror
questions.a: 1-b, 2-c, 3-a, 4-d. A periscope shows what is not directly visible, a kaleidoscope gives new patterns each time, a pinhole camera forms an image on a screen, and a plane mirror shows her face.

questions.q: Meher points her sliding pinhole camera at a distant tree on a dull evening, holds it in the open and sees nothing on the tracing paper. Which set of steps from the activity should she follow?
questions.a: Point at a distant bright object, cover head and camera with a dark cloth, and slide the smaller box. These are the steps of the sliding-camera activity.
o: Point at a distant bright object, cover head and camera with a dark cloth, and slide the smaller box
Remove the pinhole to let in more light, and keep the camera uncovered in the open evening air
Hold the camera near a candle in a lit room and slide the box away from the tracing paper
Place a plane mirror over the pinhole and look through the open side of the smaller box

questions.q: Anil says, 'A pinhole camera forms its picture because the tracing paper reflects the light back to our eye like a mirror.' (a) What does the chapter say forms the image? (b) State one feature of the image that a mirror would not give.
questions.a: (a) Light rays from the object pass through a tiny hole and form the image on the screen. (b) The pinhole image is inverted (upside down), whereas a plane mirror image is erect.
s: Part (a): rays through the tiny hole form the image on a screen
Part (b): inverted image, unlike the erect mirror image

questions.q: Chitra looks at the same tree in two ways: through a sliding pinhole camera pointed at it in bright sunlight, and in a large plane mirror held facing it. In which way does the top of the tree appear at the top of what she sees?
questions.a: Only in the plane mirror, whose image is erect. A plane mirror image is erect (left and right swapped) while a pinhole camera image is upside down.
o: Only in the plane mirror, whose image is erect
Only in the pinhole camera, whose image is erect
In both, since both show the tree upright
In neither, since both show the tree upside down

questions.q:
Tara is stuck behind a tall friend at a parade and wants to use a simple box periscope. She has a straight open box and two plane mirrors that can be fixed inside the box at a slant.
(a) Why can she not see the parade by just looking through the straight box? Use what the chapter says about how light travels.
(b) How should she fix the two mirrors to see the parade? Justify your choice.
questions.a: (a) Light travels in a straight line, and her friend blocks the straight path, so light from the parade cannot reach her eye through the straight box. (b) She should fix the mirrors in a Z-shaped arrangement, one at each end of the box; reflection from the two mirrors lets her see objects that are not visible directly.
s: Part (a): light travels in straight line and the friend blocks it
Part (b): Z-shaped placement of two mirrors, justified by reflection

questions.q: For a school exhibition you must show visitors three things: (i) how to see a game played behind a wall by looking over it, (ii) a picture of a sunlit building formed on a screen, and (iii) patterns that change every time. Choose a device for each, say what it is made of, and say what the visitor will see in (ii) and why you cannot use a plane mirror alone for (i).
questions.a: (i) A periscope: two plane mirrors in a Z-shaped box; a single plane mirror or a straight box cannot show objects around the wall, since light travels in straight lines and a periscope's two mirrors change its direction. (ii) A pinhole camera: a tiny hole and a tracing-paper screen; the visitor sees an upside-down image. (iii) A kaleidoscope: three plane mirror strips with coloured bangle pieces; reflections of reflections give new patterns when it is turned.
s: (i) periscope with two mirrors in a Z-shaped box
Why a straight box or a single mirror is not enough for (i)
(ii) pinhole camera with a tiny hole and screen
(ii) the image is upside down
(iii) kaleidoscope with three mirror strips and multiple images

questions.q:
A school stall has Rs 100 to build exhibits. Each plane mirror strip costs Rs 20. A kaleidoscope needs its mirror strips plus a Rs 10 tube. A periscope needs its mirrors plus a Rs 15 box. A pinhole camera needs two boxes at Rs 15 each plus Rs 5 of tracing paper.
(a) Using the number of mirrors the chapter's designs need, find the cost of each of the three devices.
(b) Which pairs of devices fit within Rs 100?
(c) The stall wants visitors to be surprised by something about how the picture looks. Which device in the affordable pair gives a surprising picture, and how does it look?
(d) Would you build the affordable pair or just a kaleidoscope? Weigh cost against what visitors learn.
questions.a: (a) Kaleidoscope: 3 x 20 + 10 = Rs 70. Periscope: 2 x 20 + 15 = Rs 55. Pinhole camera: 2 x 15 + 5 = Rs 35. (b) Periscope + pinhole camera = Rs 90 fits; kaleidoscope + pinhole = Rs 105 and kaleidoscope + periscope = Rs 125 do not. (c) The pinhole camera: its picture is upside down (inverted). (d) The pair costs Rs 90 and shows two different ideas (reflection and an inverted image); a kaleidoscope alone costs Rs 70 and shows changing patterns from multiple images. A reasoned choice is accepted.
s: Part (a): Rs 70, Rs 55, Rs 35 using 3 and 2 mirrors
Part (b): only periscope + pinhole camera fits (Rs 90)
Part (c): pinhole camera gives an upside-down picture
Part (d): reasoned choice weighing cost and learning

questions.q:
Ritu, a textile designer in Jaipur, is preparing a block print with two parts: a border of repeating patterns and a central scene of the city skyline. She has three tools. Tool 1: a tube with three equal mirror strips joined in a triangle and coloured bangle pieces. Tool 2: a Z-shaped box with two plane mirrors. Tool 3: two sliding boxes with a tiny hole in one and tracing paper as the screen in the other.
(a) What would she see on the tracing paper if she pointed Tool 3 at the skyline in bright sunlight?
(b) She now looks at the same skyline in a plane mirror. How does what she sees differ from the picture on the tracing paper?
(c) Why does Tool 1 give so many different patterns?
(d) Which tool would you give her for the border and which for the skyline, and what must she remember when copying from the skyline tool?
questions.a: (a) An inverted (upside-down) image of the skyline. (b) The plane mirror image is erect (not upside down) though its left and right are interchanged. (c) Reflections of reflections in three mirrors make multiple images that change when it is turned. (d) Tool 1 for the border, since it gives ever-changing patterns; Tool 3 for the skyline, remembering that its image is upside down and must be turned the right way up when copying.
s: Part (a): inverted image of the skyline
Part (b): mirror image erect with left and right interchanged
Part (c): reflections of reflections
Part (d): correct tool for each job with the inversion caution

questions.q: Radha says a kaleidoscope needs coloured bangle pieces to show any pattern at all. Mohan says that even with both ends left open and pointed at a tree it shows patterns. Decide who is right, explain what the three mirror strips do in each case, and say why a new pattern appears each time the tube is turned.
questions.a: Mohan is right: even with both ends open and pointed at a tree, one sees beautiful patterns, so the pieces are not essential. Radha is wrong. In both cases the three plane mirror strips form reflections of reflections, giving multiple images. Turning the tube changes what the mirrors reflect, so the pattern changes every time.
s: Mohan right: patterns without pieces
